extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and practising reporters learning news/obituary writing
extracted.subtask_description: Crafting news stories and obituaries about illness, death, and medical events — including sudden deaths, surgical operations, obituaries of public figures, and human-interest death reports. Emphasis on factual reporting, biography, community context, and evocative leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of the deceased
rubrics_metrics.description: State the full name of the person who died and basic identifiers such as age, occupation or public role, and place (e.g., 'Martin Engel is dead.' 'At the age of 68').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open items with a clear announcement and essential identifiers so readers immediately know who the story concerns. Examples in the text: 'Martin Engel is dead.'; 'John Howard Van Amringe...died suddenly.'; include age when available: 'At the age of 68.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause and immediate circumstances of death
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the proximate cause and the immediate circumstances surrounding the death (disease, accident, on-duty event, surgical outcome, exposure), including where and when it happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include medical causes, accident details, or situational context (e.g., 'died yesterday from heart disease', 'cause of death was pneumonia brought on by exposure', 'died yesterday on his run...'). For medical cases, describe events leading up to the critical moment (e.g., 'respiration suddenly ceased' then 'doctors massaged the heart').

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical background and career summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize birth, education, career milestones, positions held, and relevant life history that explain the subject's public importance (e.g., Van Amringe's education and long service at Columbia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise chronological biography showing why the subject mattered: birthplace, schooling, major posts, years of service, founding roles, and notable accomplishments. Examples: 'He was born at Amherst, October 11, 1842...'; 'founder, owner and editor of the Kansas City Star...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community significance and public role
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the deceased's importance to a community, institution, or movement (political leadership, philanthropy, editorial influence, neighborhood benefactor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect the individual's life to broader civic, political, or social impact: role in Tammany Hall, founding a paper, saving locals from Potter's Field, or work with the poor. Use explicit statements of significance (e.g., 'to the

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative anecdotes and vivid incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Include short, specific stories or incidents that reveal character or memorable deeds (e.g., driving in Gen. Grant's funeral, rescuing unknown victims from the Potter's Field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes provide human color and support evaluative claims; select notable, verifiable incidents that illuminate the subject's values and habits. Example anecdotes in the text: 'he drove, himself, the second coach in Gen. Grant's funeral'; 'there was a real funeral in his room for the unknown victim...and paid all the bills.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evocative lede/scene-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with a strong lede or scene that situates the reader (sensory details, small scene, or striking immediate fact) to draw interest (e.g., 'The odor from the chestnut roasters is as fragrant as ever...' or 'While joking...dropped dead').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a descriptive opening that either reports the key fact plainly or paints a short scene to engage the reader, depending on the tone: hard news ledes for sudden deaths; human-interest description for neighborhood obituaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronology of illness or events leading to death
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay out the timeline of relevant events: arrest → jail → illness; prior injury → later operation; onset of symptoms → death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear sequence so readers understand causation and progression (e.g., Tse-Ne-Gat's imprisonment then contracting the 'white man's plague'; Anton Helm's skull injury at age 5 leading to later surgery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute factual statements to authoritative sources—doctors, coroners, attorneys, judges, or named officials—especially for medical causes, legal outcomes, or procedural facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the coroner, physician, hospital, or legal counsel when available (e.g., 'Dr. Harry Czarlinsky, county coroner, said...'; 'Attorney W. J. Kershaw...appeared as counsel'). This increases credibility and allows verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanizing personal details
rubrics_metrics.description: Include small personal details that make the subject relatable: habits (smoking), possessions (books), pets (Danny the dog), mannerisms, or signature phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details such as 'He lay...among his books' or 'his pet, Danny, was curled up at the foot of the bed' add empathy and texture. Use them sparingly and relevantly to humanize without sensationalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations and reported speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Use direct quotations from the deceased (if available), acquaintances, officials, or witnesses to give immediacy and voice (e.g., 'Be sure and bring her in on time, Sam,' 'The Lord has been far better to me...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select memorable or revealing quotes that advance understanding; clearly attribute speakers and context. Quotations can serve as effective ledes or closers when they capture the subject's character or final wishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funeral, burial, and practical arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Report details about funeral services, burial place, officiants, and any public memorials or directives left by the deceased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include time/place of funeral, officiant, and burial location when known (e.g., 'The funeral will be held tomorrow afternoon at Washburn's chapel... burial in the Springfield cemetery'). These facts are often crucial for local readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survivors and family connections
rubrics_metrics.description: List immediate survivors, notable relatives, and next of kin where relevant to the story and community interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention spouse, children, close relatives, or notable ancestors (e.g., 'a niece of the late David Brewer, associate judge of the United States Supreme Court'). Include roles that explain social standing or connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual or social-historical framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the individual's life or death within larger historical, social, or political contexts (e.g., immigration waves, political machines, past massacres, reforms in prison medicine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use background to explain significance: Engel's rise as immigrant-leader in east side politics; Tse-Ne-Gat's case connected to Ute reservation and justice system. This helps readers appreciate broader relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical/technical detail when reporting operations
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering surgical operations or medical interventions, include procedural detail, immediate effects, and prognosis (e.g., description of heart massage and its timeline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accurate, specific descriptions (minutes of massage, responses observed, subsequent complications) and attribute suppositions to physicians (e.g., 'physicians say... opens up a new field in surgery'). Avoid speculation beyond expert statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral or evaluative summation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude with an assessment of character, public legacy, or moral lesson when appropriate (editorial tone limited to obituary contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obituaries in this collection sometimes offer evaluative commentary ('He was generous', 'the kind of politics accepted as legitimate...is passing'). If used, ensure evaluations are supported by examples and phrased as interpretation rather than undisputed fact.
